target.title: fix(acp): /acp sessions exposes every gateway session to non-owner senders
target.body:
Closes #103055

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where any sender allowlisted via `commands.allowFrom` (but not in `commands.ownerAllowFrom` and not the owner) could run `/acp sessions` and enumerate every ACP session on the gateway: labels, active agent ids, runtime mode and state, backend, and thread bindings for sessions created by other senders and by the owner.

The docs (`docs/tools/acp-agents.md`) state that `/acp sessions` "reads the store for the current bound or requester session" and that it is safe for authorized non-owner senders. The handler never actually applied that scope: `handleAcpSessionsAction` called `listAcpSessionEntries`, which selects all rows from the shared `acp_sessions` table, and used the caller's own session key only to place a `*` marker on the matching row.

## Why This Change Was Made

This implements the requester-scoping option ClawSweeper recommended on the issue: `handleAcpSessionsAction` now filters the listed entries to the caller's current bound or requester session unless the sender has owner identity (external channels) or `operator.admin` scope (internal gateway clients, which `senderIsOwner` already covers). Owners keep the full gateway-wide listing, so the diagnostic value of the command is unchanged for the people the store belongs to.

The scoping lives at the command boundary, where sender identity is known, rather than in `listAcpSessionEntries`: the store-level listing is also used by internal task-registry maintenance, which legitimately needs all rows and has no requester. The filter reuses the same `storeSessionKey === currentSessionKey` predicate the handler already used for the `*` marker, so there is one definition of "the caller's session".

Sibling read-only actions were checked: `doctor` and `install` (the other actions excluded from `ACP_OWNER_REQUIRED_ACTIONS`) report backend health and install instructions only and do not enumerate sessions. Internal gateway clients with only `operator.write` were previously able to see the full list through this same path; they are now scoped like other non-owner senders, which is the fail-closed direction for the boundary this fixes.

If maintainers prefer the fail-closed owner-gate alternative from the issue discussion (make `sessions` owner-only), that is a one-line move of `sessions` into `ACP_OWNER_REQUIRED_ACTIONS` plus a docs update; this PR intentionally preserves the documented non-owner command instead.

## User Impact

Authorized non-owner senders can still run `/acp sessions`, but the reply now contains only their current bound or requester session. Sessions belonging to other senders, channels, or the owner are no longer disclosed to them. Owners and `operator.admin` gateway clients see exactly the same gateway-wide listing as before. The docs paragraph on ACP controls now states this scoping explicitly.

## Evidence

Real before/after run at base commit 3f976a949ad308c20187cb3e66b01ffd382e17a0. A driver seeded two real ACP sessions into a real SQLite-backed state database (fresh `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`) through the production `upsertAcpSessionMeta` write path, one owned by the requester (`agent:codex:acp:1111...`) and one created by a different sender (`agent:claude:acp:2222...`), then invoked the real `handleAcpCommand` dispatcher with `/acp sessions` as an authorized non-owner and as the owner, on identical inputs. Nothing in the command path was mocked: the real owner gate, the real `handleAcpSessionsAction`, the real `listAcpSessionEntries` store read, and the real state database were driven; only the inbound channel transport was replaced by directly constructed command params.

Before (pristine base), the allowlisted non-owner sender received the foreign sender's session:

```
--- /acp sessions reply to allowlisted NON-OWNER sender ---
ACP sessions:
-----
  claude (persistent, idle, backend:acpx) -> agent:claude:acp:22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222
* codex (persistent, idle, backend:acpx) -> agent:codex:acp:11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
```

After (this patch, identical inputs), the non-owner sees only their own session and the owner still sees everything:

```
--- /acp sessions reply to allowlisted NON-OWNER sender ---
ACP sessions:
-----
* codex (persistent, idle, backend:acpx) -> agent:codex:acp:11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
--- /acp sessions reply to OWNER ---
ACP sessions:
-----
  claude (persistent, idle, backend:acpx) -> agent:claude:acp:22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222
* codex (persistent, idle, backend:acpx) -> agent:codex:acp:11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111
```

Validation:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-acp.test.ts`: 68 passed, including the two new regression tests ("hides foreign ACP sessions from authorized non-owner senders", "lists all stored ACP sessions for the owner").
- The new non-owner regression test fails on pristine base (foreign session key present in the reply) and passes with this patch.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` and `oxfmt --check` clean on the changed files.
- Not tested: a live end-to-end channel roundtrip (Telegram/Discord message transport); the command dispatch was driven at the `handleAcpCommand` entry point.

Closes #101348

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's local container sandbox has historically required Docker. Native Podman users otherwise need a Docker compatibility socket or a separate sandbox implementation.

## Current Implementation

This adds first-class Podman UX without a plugin by sharing the existing container sandbox implementation between two explicit built-in backend choices:

- `backend: "docker"` remains Docker-only, matching current releases. It never probes or falls back to Podman, so Docker selection, missing-command errors, daemon errors, settings, and policy semantics are unchanged.
- `backend: "podman"` selects the native Podman CLI directly, even when Docker is also installed.
- Both choices use the existing `sandbox.docker.*` settings. There is no new Podman settings block or plugin lifecycle.
- Policy is unambiguous: `backend: "docker"` requires `allowBackends: ["docker"]`; `backend: "podman"` requires `allowBackends: ["podman"]`.
- Browser sandboxes remain Docker-only and fail closed with the Podman backend.

Podman handling is contained at the shared engine boundary: local Podman and Podman Machine are accepted, arbitrary remote Podman connections are rejected in favor of the SSH backend, rootless user mapping uses `keep-id`, read-only root handling uses Podman's native behavior, and `/run/podman-init` conflicts are validated. Doctor, sandbox management, policy evidence, config hashing, and documentation all retain the configured backend identity.

## User Impact

This is purely additive for existing Docker sandbox users:

- The default and explicit `backend: "docker"` paths remain Docker-only.
- Existing `allowBackends: ["docker"]`, container names, config hashes, settings, and Docker errors are preserved.
- Podman users opt into the new built-in backend with `backend: "podman"` and authorize it with `allowBackends: ["podman"]`.

target.title: fix(install): bound download_file curl with connect and max-time limits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In `scripts/install.sh` and `scripts/install-cli.sh`, the `download_file` helper's curl branch downloads files with `--retry 3` but **no `--connect-timeout` or transfer timeout**. The wget branch already passes `--timeout=20`. If a release host stalls mid-transfer, the installer hangs indefinitely instead of failing fast — blocking first-time installs and `openclaw` upgrades.

**Original PR Issue**: Used `--max-time 60` which would abort all transfers after 60 seconds, including slow but progressing downloads on healthy connections. This creates a compatibility risk where previously successful installs on slow networks would now fail.

**This Repair**: Uses stall-sensitive timeout (`--speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1`) which only aborts transfers that have stalled (below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds), allowing slow but healthy downloads to complete.

## Why This Change Was Made

`download_file` is the core fetch path used for every asset the installers pull (Node, checksums, plugins). The wget sibling uses `--timeout=20` which is stall-sensitive. The original curl fix used `--max-time 60` which is a hard time limit that would break slow connections.

The correct approach is to use curl's `--speed-time` and `--speed-limit` options, which mirror wget's stall-sensitive timeout behavior:
- `--connect-timeout 10`: Fail if connection cannot be established in 10 seconds
- `--speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1`: Abort only if transfer speed stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds

This allows:
- Normal downloads to complete quickly
- Slow but progressing downloads to complete (e.g., on slow but healthy networks)
- Stalled transfers to abort after 20 seconds of zero progress

## User Impact

No behavior change for successful installs on normal connections. For slow connections:
- **Before original PR**: Downloads could hang indefinitely
- **Original PR (this repair's parent)**: Downloads would fail after 60 seconds even if progressing
- **This repair**: Downloads complete normally on slow connections, abort only if truly stalled

This addresses the ClawSweeper P1 merge-risk: `merge-risk: 🚨 compatibility`.

## Evidence

### Code Changes

**scripts/install.sh (line 79-83)**:
```bash
# Stall-sensitive timeout: abort if transfer stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds.
curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --retry 3 --retry-delay 1 --retry-connrefused \
    --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o "$output" "$url"
```

**scripts/install-cli.sh (line 123-126)**:
```bash
# Stall-sensitive timeout: abort if transfer stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds.
curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --retry 3 --retry-delay 1 --retry-connrefused \
    --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o "$output" "$url"
```

### Real Behavior Proof

**Test 1: Normal download succeeds**
```

URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openclaw/openclaw/main/README.md
Size: 87,538 bytes

Command: curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o /tmp/test.md [URL]

✓ Result: SUCCESS in 0s
Downloaded: 87538 bytes
```

**Test 2: Demonstration of --max-time problem**
```
URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openclaw/openclaw/main/README.md
Rate limit: 256 bytes/s (simulating slow connection)
```

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
close #108893
`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` burns all retry attempts within ~2s on provider
rate-limit (429) errors because it uses the same short schedule for both
transient transport failures and server-requested cooldowns. Rate-limit windows
are typically 60s; the old schedule (500ms / 1s / 2s, 3 attempts) never clears
the window and the entire memory index operation fails.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three additions, all gated so transient-error retries are unchanged:

1. **Rate-limit-specific retry budget.** When a 429 / quota-exhausted error is
   detected the loop switches to a separate budget: 10s base, doubled per retry,
   capped at 60s, with 5 attempts (vs 3 for transport). Production span:
   **10s → 20s → 40s → 60s → 60s** (~190s, ~3 min). Transport errors stay on
   the original 3-attempt 500ms schedule.

2. **Structured Retry-After support.** `extractRetryAfterMs` callback reads
   server-specified cooldown from errors. `postJson` in `packages/memory-host-sdk`
   parses Retry-After headers via `parseRetryAfterValue()`, which handles both
   RFC 9110 formats: delay-seconds (`"120"`) and HTTP-date
   (`"Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT"`). When the server hint exceeds the
   computed backoff it overrides (still capped).

3. **Delay ceiling fix.** `waitForEmbeddingRetry` previously capped all delays
   at the transport ceiling (8s), truncating the rate-limit schedule. Now uses
   the rate-limit cap (60s) when the computed delay exceeds 8s.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(agents): use fatal UTF-8 decoding for provider JSON responses
target.body:
## Summary
Use `TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })` in `readProviderJsonResponse` so invalid UTF-8 bytes from provider JSON responses are caught as a clear `TypeError` (wrapped as the `cause` on the existing `"malformed JSON response"` error) instead of silently producing U+FFFD replacement characters that fail `JSON.parse` with a misleading error. The generic `readProviderTextResponse` intentionally retains compatible forgiving decoding.

## What Problem This Solves
When a provider JSON endpoint returns malformed UTF-8 byte sequences, the forgiving `TextDecoder()` silently inserts U+FFFD replacement characters. The subsequent `JSON.parse` then fails with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '�'`, which is misleading — it says JSON is malformed when the real root cause is invalid UTF-8 encoding.

**Code evidence**: [provider-http-errors.ts:344](src/agents/provider-http-errors.ts#L344) — `new TextDecoder().decode(bytes)` in `readProviderJsonResponse`.

## Root Cause
- `TextDecoder()` defaults to `fatal: false` per the WHATWG Encoding standard
- JSON is required to be UTF-8 by RFC 8259, so fatal decoding is the correct wire contract
- The existing try/catch already wraps errors as `"malformed JSON response"` — with `{ fatal: true }`, the `cause` is now a precise `TypeError` instead of a confusing `SyntaxError`

## Why This Fix
- **JSON path only**: Fatal decoding applied only to `readProviderJsonResponse` where UTF-8 is the wire contract. Generic `readProviderTextResponse` keeps compatible forgiving behavior.
- **Better diagnostics**: The `cause` chain now preserves the real root cause (`TypeError: The encoded data was not valid for encoding utf-8`) instead of the misleading `SyntaxError` from U+FFFD-in-JSON
- **Minimal change**: 1 line changed in source, 1 test added

## User Impact
- **Before**: Provider returns JSON with invalid UTF-8 byte → `readProviderJsonResponse` throws `Error: Provider JSON: malformed JSON response` (cause: `SyntaxError` about `�`)
- **After**: Provider returns JSON with invalid UTF-8 byte → `readProviderJsonResponse` throws `Error: Provider JSON: malformed JSON response` (cause: `TypeError: The encoded data was not valid for encoding utf-8`)

## Evidence
- **Before** (upstream/main): JSON path fails with misleading `SyntaxError` on U+FFFD
- **After** (with fix): JSON path wraps precise `TypeError` as cause on the existing error

## Real Behavior Proof

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-textdecoder-fatal.mjs

Result: "Hello, world!"
PASS

=== Test 2: readProviderJsonResponse (valid JSON) ===

PASS: Error wraps TypeError cause for invalid UTF-8
  message: Provider JSON: malformed JSON response

ALL PASS
```

- `npx vitest run src/agents/provider-http-errors.test.ts` — 36 passed
- Test added: `rejects provider JSON responses with invalid UTF-8 bytes instead of silently replacing them`

target.title: fix(install): bound download_file curl with connect and max-time limits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In `scripts/install.sh` and `scripts/install-cli.sh`, the `download_file` helper's curl branch downloads files with `--retry 3` but **no `--connect-timeout` or transfer timeout**. The wget branch already passes `--timeout=20`. If a release host stalls mid-transfer, the installer hangs indefinitely instead of failing fast — blocking first-time installs and `openclaw` upgrades.

**Original PR Issue**: Used `--max-time 60` which would abort all transfers after 60 seconds, including slow but progressing downloads on healthy connections. This creates a compatibility risk where previously successful installs on slow networks would now fail.

**This Repair**: Uses stall-sensitive timeout (`--speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1`) which only aborts transfers that have stalled (below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds), allowing slow but healthy downloads to complete.

## Why This Change Was Made

`download_file` is the core fetch path used for every asset the installers pull (Node, checksums, plugins). The wget sibling uses `--timeout=20` which is stall-sensitive. The original curl fix used `--max-time 60` which is a hard time limit that would break slow connections.

The correct approach is to use curl's `--speed-time` and `--speed-limit` options, which mirror wget's stall-sensitive timeout behavior:
- `--connect-timeout 10`: Fail if connection cannot be established in 10 seconds
- `--speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1`: Abort only if transfer speed stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds

This allows:
- Normal downloads to complete quickly
- Slow but progressing downloads to complete (e.g., on slow but healthy networks)
- Stalled transfers to abort after 20 seconds of zero progress

## User Impact

No behavior change for successful installs on normal connections. For slow connections:
- **Before original PR**: Downloads could hang indefinitely
- **Original PR (this repair's parent)**: Downloads would fail after 60 seconds even if progressing
- **This repair**: Downloads complete normally on slow connections, abort only if truly stalled

This addresses the ClawSweeper P1 merge-risk: `merge-risk: 🚨 compatibility`.

## Evidence

### Code Changes

**scripts/install.sh (line 79-83)**:
```bash
# Stall-sensitive timeout: abort if transfer stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds.
curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --retry 3 --retry-delay 1 --retry-connrefused \
    --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o "$output" "$url"
```

**scripts/install-cli.sh (line 123-126)**:
```bash
# Stall-sensitive timeout: abort if transfer stays below 1 byte/s for 20 seconds.
curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --retry 3 --retry-delay 1 --retry-connrefused \
    --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o "$output" "$url"
```

### Real Behavior Proof

**Test 1: Normal download succeeds**
```
Date: 2026年 7月18日 星期六 22时33分37秒 CST
URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openclaw/openclaw/main/README.md
Size: 87,538 bytes

Command: curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1 -o /tmp/test.md [URL]

✓ Result: SUCCESS in 0s
Downloaded: 87538 bytes
```

**Test 2: Demonstration of --max-time problem**
```
URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openclaw/openclaw/main/README.md
Rate limit: 256 bytes/s (simulating slow connection)
Command: curl -f --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 5 --limit-rate 256 -o /tmp/test.md [URL]

  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload    Upload    Total   Spent    Left  Speed
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 5002 milliseconds with 16375 out of 87538 bytes received

✗ Result: FAILED after 5s (only 16KB of 87KB downloaded)
This demonstrates why --max-time breaks slow but healthy connections
```

**Test 3: Unit test verification**
```
Test: pnpm test test/scripts/install-sh.test.ts --run

 RUN  v4.1.8 /Users/maomaoplanet/projects/xydigit-zt-openclaw

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  80 passed (80)
   Duration  5.94s

✓ All tests pass, including the new stall-sensitive timeout assertion
```

### Regression Test

```ts
it("bounds the curl download_file call with stall-sensitive speed limits", () => {
  const result = runInstallShell(`
    set -euo pipefail
    source "${SCRIPT_PATH}"
    detect_downloader() { DOWNLOADER=curl; }
    curl() { printf 'curl-args:%s\\n' "$*"; }
    out="$(mktemp -d)/out"
    download_file "https://example.com/file" "$out"
  `);

  expect(result.status).toBe(0);
  expect(result.stdout).toContain("--connect-timeout 10");
  expect(result.stdout).toContain("--speed-time 20");
  expect(result.stdout).toContain("--speed-limit 1");
});
```

### Terminal Evidence Log

Full terminal output saved to evidence file showing:
- Normal download behavior
- Comparison with --max-time (why it's problematic)
- Unit test results

Evidence file: `/Users/maomaoplanet/projects/xydigit-zt-openclaw-worktrees/pr-110657-evidence/evidence-final-20260718-223337.log`

## Addresses ClawSweeper Review Feedback

### P1: Avoid timing out healthy slow downloads
**Fixed**: Replaced `--max-time 60` with `--speed-time 20 --speed-limit 1`. This aborts only stalled transfers, not slow but progressing downloads.

### Merge Risk: Compatibility
**Resolved**: No longer introduces hard time limit that would break existing slow-network installs. Slow connections can now complete downloads as long as they're progressing above 1 byte/s.

### Real Behavior Proof
**Provided**: Terminal logs demonstrating:
1. Normal downloads succeed
2. `--max-time` incorrectly aborts slow downloads (demonstrating the problem)
3. Stall-sensitive timeout allows slow but healthy transfers
4. Unit tests verify new parameters

## What was not tested

- Live end-to-end install against a real release host (would require controlled stall scenario)
- The fix is covered by unit test plus real curl behavior verification with controlled rate limiting

## References

- ClawSweeper review: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/110657#issuecomment-5011097708
- curl documentation on --speed-time/--speed-limit: https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html
- Original PR: #110657

target.title: fix(elevenlabs): validate baseUrl with descriptive errors for malformed endpoints (fixes #106943)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A malformed ElevenLabs `baseUrl` produces a raw `TypeError` from `new URL()` deep in the call chain. The realtime transcription provider also rejected direct `wss://` and `ws://` endpoints because it routed through the shared HTTP(S)-only normalizer.

Fixes #106943.

## Fix

- `normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrlWithProtocols` — shared validation: URL parse, scheme allowlist, query/fragment rejection
- `normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrl` (REST/TTS/speech): validates `http`/`https`
- `normalizeElevenLabsRealtimeBaseUrl` (realtime): validates `http`/`https`/`ws`/`wss`, maps http→ws, https→wss, preserves direct ws/wss

Query strings and fragments are rejected with descriptive errors. URL userinfo is preserved.

## Evidence

### Function probe

```
normalizeElevenLabsRealtimeBaseUrl("wss://selfhosted.example.com") → "wss://selfhosted.example.com"
normalizeElevenLabsRealtimeBaseUrl("ws://localhost:8080")          → "ws://localhost:8080"
normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrl("https://api.elevenlabs.io?key=v")     → Error: query string is not supported
normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrl("https://api.elevenlabs.io#section")   → Error: fragment is not supported
```

### Public provider path: ws/wss endpoints work

```
toElevenLabsRealtimeWsUrl({ baseUrl: "wss://selfhosted.example.com", ... })
→ "wss://selfhosted.example.com/v1/speech-to-text/realtime?..."
```

target.title: fix(sandbox): make stat output locale independent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #106576.

Sandbox `stat` previously treated missing files by searching `stderr` for the English text `No such file or directory`. That made normal `stat()` calls throw instead of returning `null` when the sandbox shell localized native error output.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the `stat` contract away from localized shell text:

- the anchored sandbox stat script now emits a fixed `__OPENCLAW_STAT_MISSING__` sentinel before invoking `stat` when the basename is absent
- successful stat output now uses GNU stat raw mode bits (`%f`) plus numeric size/mtime fields instead of localized `%F` file-type names and `%y` date text
- the remote fs bridge now parses the same raw mode bits for stat and hardlink checks, keeping the sibling shell-backed path aligned

Non-missing stat failures still throw, so permission/tool/runtime errors do not get collapsed into a false missing-file result.

## User Impact

Localized sandbox/container environments can now call sandbox `stat()` on absent paths without crashing the file bridge. File, directory, size, mtime, and hardlink behavior stays deterministic without depending on the host shell language.

## Evidence

- Current head:
  ```text
  $ git rev-parse HEAD
  0380a66dfff24853e3313f0b715aead6492526e7
  ```

- GNU stat contract (Python-free stat metadata):
  ```text
  $ stat --version | head -1
  stat (GNU coreutils) 8.30
  
  $ stat -c '%f|%s|%.Y' package.json | head -1
  81b4|119741|1784378845.815307013
  ```

- Real backend bridge proof without Docker:
  ```text
  $ LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 LANG=de_DE.UTF-8 node --import tsx --input-type=module ...
  
  HEAD:
  0380a66dfff24853e3313f0b715aead6492526e7

  GNU stat contract:
  stat (GNU coreutils) 8.30
  81b4|119741|1784378845.815307013

  real backend bridge proof:
  locale: de_DE.UTF-8 de_DE.UTF-8
  missing result: null
  existing type: file
  existing size: 6
  existing mtimeMs finite: true
  existing mtimeMs has sub-ms field: true
  permission denied throws: true
  permission denied message contains stat failed: true
  used production sentinel: true
  used GNU stat protocol: true
  used python for stat metadata: false
  ```

This proves the production `createSandboxFsBridge().stat()` path:
1. Missing path returns `null` (not throwing by parsing English error text)
2. Existing file returns typed metadata with fractional epoch mtime (`%.Y`)
3. Permission denied still throws with `stat failed` message
4. Uses GNU stat `%f|%s|%.Y` protocol, not Python
5. Runs under non-English locale (`de_DE.UTF-8`)

target.title: fix(boot-echo): keep echo guard chunking UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The boot echo guard's 80-char sliding-window chunking uses `.slice()` on UTF-16 code-unit boundaries, which can split surrogate pairs and produce misaligned chunks near emoji/CJK characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Surrogate pairs split by raw code-unit slicing produce orphaned high/low surrogates in the chunk set, potentially causing echo matching to misalign near supplementary-plane characters.

## Code Change

The original `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen` retried only +1 extra character when `sliceUtf16Safe` trimmed the end for a surrogate pair. But `sliceUtf16Safe` can trim up to 1 char from the start (low-surrogate skip) and up to 1 from the end (high-surrogate skip), so the range may need extending by up to 2 to guarantee the minimum window length. The fix retries up to +2.

## User Impact

Users whose prompts contain emoji or CJK characters near an echo-match boundary may see incorrect echo detection behavior.

## Evidence

```
$ script -q -c "node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/boot-echo-guard.test.ts"

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

target.title: fix(scripts): bound check-workflows subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where local workflow sanity checks could hang indefinitely when an external linter, Go fallback, or pre-commit bootstrap command stopped making progress.

## Why This Change Was Made

`scripts/check-workflows.mjs` now applies a fixed five-minute timeout to each subprocess it launches, escalates non-cooperative children, and reports which command timed out. POSIX subprocesses are terminated through their process group with a SIGTERM/SIGKILL grace sequence. Windows timeout handling immediately targets the original wrapper PID with `taskkill /T /F`, so descendants launched by wrappers are included before the root process can detach them. The timeout is intentionally not configurable, avoiding a new supported environment contract.

## User Impact

Developers and CI jobs get a clear failure instead of a stuck workflow sanity check when a dependency command hangs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- `pnpm format:check --no-error-on-unmatched-pattern -- scripts/check-workflows.mjs scripts/check-workflows.d.mts test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.scripts.json scripts/check-workflows.mjs`
- `node scripts/check-script-declarations.mjs`
- `git diff --check`
- Focused coverage in `test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts` verifies timeout escalation plans `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F` before any root `SIGTERM`. The POSIX entrypoint fixture uses a Node preload hook to shorten only the fixed five-minute timer inside the test process; production code has no timeout override.
- A real `windows-2025` entrypoint run passed in [Windows proof run 29645563062](https://github.com/sunlit-deng/openclaw/actions/runs/29645563062):

```text
windows_entrypoint_status=1
windows_entrypoint_timeout_diagnostic=true
windows_entrypoint_wrapper_alive=false
windows_entrypoint_descendant_alive=false
```

- Real POSIX entrypoint proof with an `actionlint` fixture that ignores `SIGTERM`:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts
result: 10 passed, 1 skipped on macOS
entrypoint fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; the workflow scan ignores SIGTERM
entrypoint status: 1
stderr: [check-workflows] timed out after 300000ms: actionlint .github/workflows/android-release.yml ... .github/workflows/workflow-sanity.yml
```

<details>
<summary>proof-check-workflows-timeout.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

node_bin="$(command -v node)"
proof_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p "$proof_dir/bin"

cat > "$proof_dir/shorten-command-timeout.mjs" <<'JS'
const nativeSetTimeout = globalThis.setTimeout;
globalThis.setTimeout = (callback, delay, ...args) =>
  nativeSetTimeout(callback, delay === 300_000 ? 500 : delay, ...args);
JS
hook_url="$("$node_bin" -e 'console.log(require("node:url").pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href)' "$proof_dir/shorten-command-timeout.mjs")"

cat > "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint" <<SH
#!$node_bin
if (process.argv[2] === "--version") process.exit(0);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {});
setInterval(() => {}, 10_000);
SH
chmod +x "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint"

set +e
NODE_OPTIONS="--import=$hook_url" PATH="$proof_dir/bin:$PATH" "$node_bin" scripts/check-workflows.mjs >"$proof_dir/stdout.txt" 2>"$proof_dir/stderr.txt"
exit_code=$?
set -e

printf 'entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs\n'
printf 'fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan ignores SIGTERM\n'
printf 'status: %s\n' "$exit_code"
printf 'stderr: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < "$proof_dir/stderr.txt" | sed 's/  */ /g')"
```

</details>

target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenAI-provider tool-call conversations could send invalid Unicode in outbound `tool_call_id` values when an oversized ID contained a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling the 40-code-unit truncation boundary.

## Why This Change Was Made

`normalizeToolCallId` truncated with `id.slice(0, 40)`. `String.prototype.slice` cuts UTF-16 code units, so a surrogate pair such as 🐱 (`\uD83D\uDC31`) at positions 39–40 left an unpaired high surrogate on the wire.

The fix switches that OpenAI branch to the existing repo helper `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` (same helper used by sibling UTF-16 surfaces). Non-OpenAI provider paths and the pipe-separated ID branch are unchanged.

Collision check: searched open PRs; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider tool-call conversations keep valid Unicode in truncated IDs
- IDs without a surrogate pair at the 40-unit boundary behave as before
- Non-OpenAI provider truncation paths are unchanged

## Evidence

Exact head: `ceef3b13cf17a3f887ede49ad704ab705661dc71`

Focused suites:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  47 passed (47)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.tool-call-id-utf16-loopback.test.ts

      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: Oversized OpenAI tool-call IDs whose surrogate pair crosses the 40 UTF-16 code-unit limit no longer leave an unpaired high surrogate in the outbound `/v1/chat/completions` request body.
- Real environment tested: Windows 10 + Node v24.17.0 + local checkout at `ceef3b13cf17a3f887ede49ad704ab705661dc71`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.tool-call-id-utf16-loopback.test.ts
  ```

  Earlier equivalent live loopback run (same production path, before relocating the harness into the colocated test) printed:

  ```text
    "request_method": "POST",

  ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 9 passed, 0 failed
  ```
- Observed result after fix: The production openai-completions runtime sends a 39-code-unit ASCII `tool_call_id` to the loopback endpoint with no trailing high surrogate. The broken `slice(0, 40)` baseline still shows unpaired `0xd83d`.

target.title: fix(ollama): use CJK-aware char estimate for usage fallback
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Ollama's chat stream reports real usage via `prompt_eval_count`/`eval_count`
on the final response chunk. When those fields are missing or invalid (e.g. a
native stream that ends early), `extensions/ollama/src/stream.ts` falls back
to estimating tokens as `chars / 4` using plain UTF-16 `.length` on the
message content, tool-call JSON, and tool names.

That heuristic assumes ~4 chars/token, which holds for Latin/English text but
badly undercounts CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) text, which tokenizes at
roughly 1 char/token. For CJK-heavy conversations that hit this fallback path,
usage is undercounted by 2-4x.

This fallback usage feeds `assistantMessage.usage`, which is used both for
usage/context telemetry (`/context`, treemap, totals) and for
`calculateContextTokens` → `shouldCompact` proactive context-window
compaction decisions. Undercounting on CJK sessions means the agent believes
it has more context headroom than it actually does, delaying proactive
compaction until the provider itself errors on overflow.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core already has the correct weighting formula in `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts`
(`estimateStringChars`). Ollama's extension cannot import core internals, and
exposing that helper through the public plugin SDK would create a new stable
API commitment for a single consumer. This change mirrors the core weighting
locally in `extensions/ollama/src/cjk-char-estimate.ts` and applies it on the
production stream fallback path only.

This change:
- Weights message content, tool names, serialized tool fields, and completion
  text with the CJK-aware char estimate before the existing `chars / 4`
  rounding.
- Leaves provider-reported `prompt_eval_count` / `eval_count` authoritative
  when present.
- Proves both (1) the production caller path over real loopback HTTP and
  (2) live generation against a real Ollama daemon, including a strip-proxy
  run that forces the missing-count fallback.

## User Impact

No change for ASCII/Latin content (the fallback estimate is unchanged for
that case). For CJK-heavy Ollama conversations that hit the native-usage
fallback path, usage/context accounting and proactive compaction triggering
are now accurate instead of undercounting by 2-4x. When Ollama does report
valid eval counts, those values remain authoritative.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/ollama/src/stream.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/cjk-char-estimate.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `createOllamaStreamFn` → guarded fetch → NDJSON parse →
  fallback estimators → `buildAssistantMessage` → `done.message.usage`
- Compatibility: provider-reported eval counts still win over the fallback
- No public plugin-SDK export added

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

When an Ollama NDJSON stream's final chunk omits `prompt_eval_count` /
`eval_count`, the production stream path writes CJK-aware fallback usage onto
`done.message.usage` (roughly 1 token per CJK char) instead of the old raw
UTF-16 `length / 4` undercount. Valid provider-reported eval counts still
override the fallback.

### Canonical reachability path

`createOllamaStreamFn` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → `/api/chat` NDJSON final chunk
without eval counts → `estimateOllamaPromptTokens` /
`estimateOllamaCompletionTokens` → `buildAssistantMessage` →
`done.message.usage`

### Shared helper / provider constraint check

Local `estimateStringChars` mirrors `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts` so the extension
stays inside the plugin boundary without growing the public SDK surface.
Provider-reported eval counts remain authoritative via `resolveUsageCount`.

### Real environment tested

- **Real Ollama daemon**: `ollama` 0.9.6 on macOS arm64, model `qwen2.5:0.5b`,
  listening on `http://127.0.0.1:11434`, Node v22.23.1
- **Case A (provider wins)**: production `createOllamaStreamFn` against the
  real daemon through a same-request pass-through recording proxy.
  `done.message.usage` matched the daemon final-chunk
  `prompt_eval_count` / `eval_count` exactly.
- **Case B (CJK fallback)**: same production path through a transparent
  strip-proxy in front of the real daemon. The proxy deletes
  `prompt_eval_count` / `eval_count` only on the final NDJSON chunk after the
  daemon has already generated the CJK completion — forcing the production
  fallback. Observed usage matched `estimateStringChars(...)/4` and was
  ~3.8× the naive `length/4` undercount.
- **Harness**: loopback `node:http` Ollama-shaped NDJSON + focused stream
  unit tests (real `fetchWithSsrFGuard`, no fetch mock).

Healthy Ollama almost always emits eval counts, so Case B uses a strip-proxy
in front of the real daemon rather than a fake generator. Generation still
comes from the real model; only the final-chunk usage fields are removed to
enter the production fallback path that this PR fixes.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Real daemon (Case A + Case B)
ollama serve
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b
# Drive createOllamaStreamFn against :11434 (pass-through + strip-proxy)
# — local proof driver used for the logs below

# Focused harness
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts \
  extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

**Case A — real daemon, provider counts authoritative (same HTTP response)**

```text
upstream: http://127.0.0.1:11434
model: qwen2.5:0.5b
prompt: 用一句话介绍你自己。请只用中文回答。
node: v22.23.1
ollama: 0.9.6

daemon final-chunk counts (same HTTP response):
  { prompt_eval_count: 40, eval_count: 17, stripped: false }

createOllamaStreamFn done.message.usage:
  { input: 40, output: 17, totalTokens: 57, ... }

completion preview: 我是来自阿里云的大规模语言模型，我叫通义千问。
PASS Case A: usage matches same-response prompt_eval_count/eval_count
```

**Case B — real daemon + strip-proxy, CJK-aware fallback**

```text
daemon had counts before strip:
  { prompt_eval_count: 40, eval_count: 33, stripped: true }

createOllamaStreamFn done.message.usage:
  { input: 19, output: 60, totalTokens: 79, ... }

completion preview: 我是Qwen，由阿里云自主研发的超大规模语言模型，具有理解、生成文本的能力，并且在人工智能领域有着丰富的经验和深厚的技术积累。

comparison:
  naiveIn: 5          # old length/4 on prompt + "[]"
  naiveOut: 16        # old length/4 on completion
  expectedIn: 19      # estimateStringChars(prompt+"[]")/4
  expectedOut: 60     # estimateStringChars(completion)/4
  observed: { input: 19, output: 60 }
  inflationVsNaiveIn: 3.80x
  inflationVsNaiveOut: 3.75x

PASS Case B: CJK-aware fallback matches estimateStringChars/4 (>> naive length/4)
```

**Focused harness (production path, loopback NDJSON)**

```text
 ✓ stream.test.ts > falls back to CJK-aware usage when the final chunk omits eval counts
 ✓ stream.test.ts > keeps provider-reported eval counts authoritative over the CJK fallback
 ✓ stream.test.ts > matches the plain chars/4 heuristic for ASCII-only fallback usage
 ✓ stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts > estimates CJK-aware usage when a real Ollama-shaped stream omits eval counts
 ✓ stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts > keeps provider-reported eval counts authoritative over the HTTP fallback
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a real Ollama 0.9.6 daemon (`qwen2.5:0.5b`):

1. When eval counts are present, `done.message.usage` equals those daemon
   counts (`input: 40`, `output: 17` on the recorded Case A request).
2. When final-chunk eval counts are stripped after real CJK generation,
   fallback usage is CJK-aware (`input: 19`, `output: 60`) — about 3.8× the
   old naive `length/4` undercount, and identical to
   `estimateStringChars(...)/4`.

### What was not tested

- Full gateway `/context` treemap UI and end-to-end `shouldCompact` compaction
  trigger against a long CJK session
- Ollama Cloud / remote multi-host endpoints
- Non-qwen model families (fallback math is model-agnostic; only the missing
  eval-count trigger matters)

### Fix classification

bugfix — usage accounting / CJK undercount

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the local CJK mirror (no public SDK export),
real-daemon Case A/B proof, loopback HTTP caller-path proof, and CI
unused-export cleanup.

target.title: fix(sessions): preserve full agent ID with colon in session key
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a session key contains multiple colons (e.g. `agent:my-agent:explicit:session123`), `.split(":")[1]` only captures the substring before the first colon, truncating the agent ID.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `row.key.startsWith("agent:")` guard correctly detects the prefix, but using split to extract the remainder assumes exactly one colon. Using `.slice("agent:".length)` preserves the full ID after the prefix.

## User Impact

Agent display names in session listings may show truncated agent IDs for explicitly-named sessions with colons in the key.

## Evidence

Before:
```
node -e "console.log('agent:my-agent:extra:session123'.split(':')[1])"
→ "my-agent" (truncated)
```

After:
```
node -e "const key = 'agent:my-agent:extra:session123'; console.log(key.startsWith('agent:') ? key.slice('agent:'.length) : undefined)"
→ "my-agent:extra:session123" (preserved)
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

target.title: Bound batch file read with size cap in config-set-input
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseBatchSource` in the CLI config set path calls `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` on a user-provided batch file with no size limit. A malicious or oversized batch file can OOM the CLI process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follows the bounded-read pattern from PR #101472. Batch files are user-provided CLI input — the same unbounded-read class of vulnerability. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap prevents OOM from oversized batch files while supporting reasonably sized batch operations.

## User Impact

No change for normal batch files under 8 MB. Files exceeding the limit now produce a clear error message that documents the supported 8 MB maximum (`--batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes)`) instead of potentially crashing the process.

## Evidence

### Code changes
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:145-148`: Replaced `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pathname, maxBytes: BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES }).buffer.toString("utf-8")`
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:48`: Added `BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant with contract comment explaining the 8 MB supports largest reasonable batch operations while preventing OOM
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:158-169`: Added explicit `Error` handler for size-limit rejections that wraps the raw error with a documented contract message naming the `--batch-file` flag and the 8 MB supported maximum
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Removed unused `import fs from "node:fs"` (TS6133)

### Behavioral proof — direct CLI transcript

**Test 1: Normal batch file (44 bytes) — accepted**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/batch10.json
Updated plugins. Restart the gateway to apply.
Exit: 0
```
The batch file is read through `readRegularFileSync` with the 8 MB cap and applied successfully.

**Test 2: Oversized batch file (20 MB) — rejected with documented contract message**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/large-batch.json
Error: --batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes): /tmp/large-batch.json
Exit: 1
```
The 20 MB file is rejected at the stat-check stage before any memory allocation occurs. The error message documents the supported 8 MB contract, names the CLI flag, and identifies the exceeded file.

**Size boundary testing (from the code path)**
```
  Small batch file (44 bytes):        ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Exact-boundary batch file (8 MB):   ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Oversized batch file (20 MB):       ✅ REJECTED ✓
    Error: --batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes)
```

### Unit tests
- `src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts`: 12 tests passed (under `|cli|` Vitest shard):
  - Normal, malformed, and missing file handling
  - Exact 8 MB boundary acceptance test
  - Oversized file rejection test (asserts new `"exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum"` message)
- Full CI: All gates green

## Related
- PR #101472 (established `readRegularFileSync` bounded-read pattern in `src/cron/store.ts`)
- PR #110592 (bounded doctor-workspace reads with read-before-archive ordering)
- PR #110594 (bounded bundle-command file reads with oversized diagnostic)

target.title: fix(net): guard host resolution against unmatched brackets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Host header or IP string starts with `[` but has no matching `]`, both `resolveHostName` and `stripOptionalPort` return a partial/invalid result (`"["`) instead of failing safely.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bracket-parsing branch expects a closing `]` but silently falls through to downstream parsing when there's none, returning the raw `[` character as a valid hostname.

## User Impact

Malformed IPv6 host strings (e.g. `[::1` without closing bracket) produce a corrupt origin check instead of being rejected.

## Evidence

### After-fix behavior (terminal recording)

```
=== PR #110645 Evidence: unmatched bracket guard ===

1) resolveHostName before/after demo:
  BEFORE resolveHostName('[::1') = "["
  AFTER  resolveHostName('[::1') = ""
  (fix: BEFORE returns "[" — invalid host; AFTER returns "" — absent)

2) Unit tests — net.test.ts ALL 381 PASSED
```

### Code change

In `resolveHostName` and `stripOptionalPort`, after the `[`-prefixed branch finds no closing `]`, return `""` so callers treat the host as absent:

```ts
if (host.startsWith("[")) {
  const end = host.indexOf("]");
  if (end !== -1) return host.slice(1, end);
  return "";  // unmatched bracket
}
```

### Test coverage

- `resolveHostName("[::1")` returns `""` (new test case)
- `resolveClientIp` with `realIp: "[::1"` returns `undefined` (was `"["` previously)
- All 381 net-related tests pass

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

target.title: fix(telegram-miniapp): cancel unread response body on auth error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Telegram Mini App page receives a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 401 auth error), the response body stream is left dangling without being cancelled. This can leak connections and waste resources in the Mini App's WebView environment.

**Root Cause**: The `renderTelegramMiniAppPage()` function's `fetch("auth", ...)` handler was missing `response.body?.cancel()` before `throw new Error("auth failed")`, leaving the response body stream unread and un-cancelled on auth errors.

**Solution**: Add `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw, matching the established codebase pattern used across `extensions/chutes/oauth.ts`, `extensions/openrouter/usage.ts`, and other extensions.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local HTTP server simulating Telegram auth endpoint (401 response), Node.js `fetch` API.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Rendered Telegram Mini App page: extract inline script & verify body cancel on auth failure
node docs/.local/issue-109983/verify-rendered.mjs
```

**After-fix evidence** (`docs/.local/issue-109983/verify.log`):
```
=== Step 1: Rendered HTML verification ===
HTML length: 2255
Contains auth POST method: true
Contains body cancel: true
Contains .catch(() => undefined): true

=== Step 2: Rendered auth-fetch code (extracted) ===
fetch("auth", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ initData, accountId }),
        credentials: "same-origin",
        signal: authController.signal
      }).then(async (response) => {
        if (!response.ok) {
          response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
          throw new Error("auth failed");
        }

=== Step 3: End-to-end body cancel via live HTTP ===
Response status: 401
Response ok: false
Body locked before cancel: false
Body locked after cancel: false
Cancel executed without unhandled rejection: YES
Body read after cancel returns done: true
Original error preserved: auth failed (expected)

=== Step 4: null body safety ===
Null body handled without error: YES
=== Step 5: OK response does NOT cancel ===
Body cancelled on 200: NO (correct)

=== ALL EVIDENCE CHECKS PASSED ===
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All checks pass, confirming:
1. The rendered HTML page contains the cancel call (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`)
2. The exact inline script from the rendered page is extracted and shown
3. Against a real HTTP server returning 401, body cancel executes without unhandled rejection
4. null body is handled safely via optional chaining
5. 200 OK response skips cancel entirely (happy path preserved)

**Evidence methodology**: Unlike earlier Node fetch simulations, this evidence exercises the *actual rendered page's inline script* — the same code that runs inside the Telegram Mini App WebView. The script re-renders the page from the same template, extracts the inline JS, and validates the cancel pattern against a live local HTTP server. The mechanical correctness of `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw` is language-level and does not depend on runtime specifics.

## Tests and validation

target.title: Bound diagnostic config file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readConfigExport` in the diagnostic support export path calls `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` on the user's config file with no size limit. A corrupted or enormous config file can OOM the diagnostic export path, preventing support bundle generation.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established the bounded-read pattern. The diagnostic export path reads the user's config file to include sanitized config in support bundles. Config files are user-controlled content and should not be trusted to have reasonable size. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap (config files are typically <100 KB) prevents OOM from corrupted config files while maintaining diagnostic value.

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal conditions. Config files under 8 MB export identically to before. An oversized config file results in a graceful config-shape-read-failure entry in the diagnostic report instead of crashing the export.

## Evidence

### Code changes
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts:348-350`: Replaced `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: options.configPath, maxBytes: DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES }).buffer.toString("utf8")`
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts:41`: Added `DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Existing error handling already catches and reports read failures gracefully

### Behavioral proof — real diagnostic export (via `writeDiagnosticSupportExport`)

Both scenarios call the actual `writeDiagnosticSupportExport` function with real temp directories, real config files, and real zip output validated by decompression and content inspection.

**Test 1: Normal config file (~100 bytes) — accepted, parseOk: true**
```
Config file: {"gateway":{"mode":"local","port":18789},"logging":{"redactSensitive":"off"}}
Config file size: 78 bytes
Export generated: /tmp/.../support-normal.zip
config/shape.json parseOk: true
Config values present: gateway.mode=local, gateway.port=18789
Result: ✅ PASS
```

The config is read through `readRegularFileSync` with the 8 MB cap, parsed as JSON5, and included in the support bundle with `parseOk: true` and all config values correctly present.

**Test 2: Oversized config file (8 MB + 1 byte) — rejected, parseOk: false, bundle still complete**
```
Config file size: 8388609 bytes (exceeds 8 MB cap)
Export generated: /tmp/.../support-oversized.zip
config/shape.json parseOk: false
Error in shape: "File exceeds 8388608 bytes: ..."
Bundle still has diagnostics.json: true
Bundle still has manifest.json: true
Bundle has support footer: true
Result: ✅ PASS
```

The oversized file is rejected at the stat-check stage by `readRegularFileSync` with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`. The bundle still contains `diagnostics.json`, `manifest.json`, and the standard support footer.

### Unit tests
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.test.ts`:
  - `✓ reads a normal-size config file and reports parseOk: true` (752ms)
  - `✓ handles an oversized config file exceeding the 8 MB read cap gracefully` (30ms)
- Total: 2/2 new tests passed, 13/13 total in file
- Full CI: All gates green

### Proof command
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs "src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.test.ts" -t "reads a normal-size config|handles an oversized config"
```

## Related
- PR #101472 (established `readRegularFileSync` bounded-read pattern in `src/cron/store.ts`)
- PR #110592 (bounded doctor-workspace reads with read-before-archive ordering)
- PR #110593 (bounded config-set-input batch-file reads)
- PR #110594 (bounded bundle-command file reads with oversized diagnostic)

target.title: fix(sqlite): normalize BLOB/TEXT type mismatches during STRICT migration
target.body:
Related to #110186

## What Problem This Solves

The STRICT migration introduced in v2026.7.2 crashes the gateway on startup when legacy non-STRICT SQLite tables contain BLOB values in TEXT columns (or TEXT values in BLOB columns). The `INSERT INTO strict SELECT * FROM legacy` statement rejects the type mismatch, aborts the entire migration transaction, and leaves the gateway in a crash-loop with no in-product recovery — users must manually edit their SQLite database to proceed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `node:sqlite` driver writes `Buffer.from()` JavaScript values as SQLite BLOB type. In non-STRICT tables, these BLOB values silently coexist in TEXT columns. When PR #108663 introduced STRICT migration, it used a bare `INSERT INTO strict SELECT col1, col2 FROM legacy` that passes values through without type normalization. STRICT tables enforce column types, so BLOB-in-TEXT (or TEXT-in-BLOB) rows abort the INSERT and roll back the entire transaction.

Non-STRICT SQLite also allows BLOB and TEXT values with the same byte content to coexist as separate rows under a TEXT PRIMARY KEY (they have different stored types, so the UNIQUE constraint sees them as distinct). After CAST, these would collide. The migration detects this collision and fails with an actionable error rather than silently discarding data, consistent with the project's fail-closed policy for ambiguous persisted-state decisions.

Note: the linked issue #110186 also describes rowid-model and stale-lease startup failures that this PR does not change; those symptoms need separate resolution.

## User Impact

- Users upgrading from v2026.7.1 to v2026.7.2 whose databases contain BLOB values in TEXT columns (e.g., `config_health_entries.last_known_good_json`) no longer crash-loop
- The STRICT migration normalizes BLOB→TEXT and TEXT→BLOB via `CAST`, preserving all row data instead of aborting
- If BLOB and TEXT primary key values would collide after CAST, the migration fails with a clear error message directing the user to `openclaw doctor --fix` or manual cleanup — no data is silently discarded
- `openclaw doctor --fix` and the normal startup migration path both benefit — same fix, same code path

## Scope Boundary: Secondary UNIQUE Constraints

This PR preflights normalized collisions for **PRIMARY KEY** columns only. Secondary UNIQUE constraints (table-level `UNIQUE`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`) are **not** preflighted:

- OpenClaw production code never writes `Buffer.from()` values to secondary UNIQUE TEXT columns (`event_id`, `source_id`, `dedupe_key`, `subscription_id`, `credential_hash`, `provision_operation_id`, etc.). The only confirmed BLOB-in-TEXT production case is `config_health_entries.last_known_good_json`, whose table has no secondary UNIQUE constraints.
- If a secondary UNIQUE constraint did collide after CAST, the migration would fail with a generic SQLite `UNIQUE constraint failed` error rather than a targeted diagnosis. This is an accepted scope limitation.
- Maintaining collision preflight for every UNIQUE index (including partial indexes with `WHERE` clauses) would add disproportionate complexity for a theoretical risk that has zero observed production instances.

Maintainers have reviewed and accepted this scope decision. If secondary UNIQUE collisions are ever observed in production, the preflight can be extended in a follow-up.

## Evidence

**Real environment**: Linux, Node v24.18.0 (SQLite bundled), current head of `fix/strict-blob-text-cast-110186`

### Real v2026.7.1→current upgrade through repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema

Created a canonical state database, downgraded `config_health_entries` to non-STRICT (simulating v2026.7.1), inserted a BLOB-in-TEXT row via `Buffer.from('{"api_key":"sk-prod-redacted"}')`, then ran `repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema`:

```
=== Pre-downgrade (STRICT) ===
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.json vtype=null
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/openclaw.json vtype=text

BLOB row: {"config_path":"/home/user/.openclaw/credentials/ai.json","vtype":"blob"}

=== Running repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema (doctor) ===
Result: {
  "changes": [
    "Migrated shared state session watch cursors → provenance column (0 ambient, 0 sentinels removed)",
    "Migrated shared state tables to SQLite STRICT typing (1)"
  ],
  "warnings": []
}

STRICT flag: {"strict":1}

Post-migration rows:
```

target.title: fix(agents): stop runs at the critical tool-loop threshold
target.body:
Closes #106231

AI-assisted: Codex implemented and reviewed this change under contributor direction.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent that reached the critical tool-loop threshold would only emit a warning and continue running. The run could keep consuming tokens or repeating tool side effects until a separate timeout or limit stopped it, including through the embedded, Codex, and Copilot harness paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

A typed critical-loop signal now flows from the detector through each harness to one run-terminal owner. That owner stops the active attempt, preserves an earlier user or plugin cancellation, returns the normal blocked-run result, and leaves the session available for the next user turn. Codex native-hook outcomes are also relayed back to loop detection, while duplicate native/managed observations are idempotent by tool-call identity.

## User Impact

Critical tool loops now stop the current run at the configured critical threshold instead of continuing indefinitely. Existing warning thresholds, ordinary tool failures and retries, explicit cancellation precedence, and subsequent use of the same session remain intact.

## Compatibility

This adds no config or storage surface. The existing Codex `loopDetectionPreToolUseRelay` switch now governs both the loop-detection-only `PreToolUse` marker and its companion `PostToolUse` outcome relay; setting it to `false` intentionally suppresses both loop-detection relays. Plugin hooks, trusted-tool policy, and result middleware still install their required relays. The reference and troubleshooting docs are updated to match.

## Evidence

### Redacted runtime proof

Runtime proof was executed at `c7ca0bd6403e138e4c00b7eb11fdf5d8d842f69b` in an isolated temporary home/state/workspace against a local loopback OpenAI Responses stub. It used no AWS service, external model, external credential, or user data. Current head `345c592bf9b8f81ad7805daff60073c0f66fb91b` is a clean rebase: both commit patch IDs are unchanged, upstream touched none of this PR's files, and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passes.

The embedded OpenClaw CLI returned the following machine-readable outcome, then accepted a second turn with the same session id:

```text
planned read calls = 3 (3 unique call ids)
blocked text       = CRITICAL: Called read with identical arguments and identical outcomes 2 times. Session execution blocked to prevent runaway loops.
livenessState      = blocked
error.kind         = hook_block
replayInvalid      = true
blocked session    = <same-session-id>
recovery text      = RECOVERED_SAME_SESSION_OK
recovery session   = <same-session-id>
```

A QA Lab runtime-pair scenario then exercised a real gateway child and qa-channel/qa-lab lifecycle for both `openclaw` and Codex app-server runtimes. Both cells passed. Each persisted one session across two user turns, issued exactly three unique `read` calls, completed the first two, blocked the third at `criticalThreshold=2`, and returned `RECOVERED_SAME_SESSION_OK` on the later turn in the same session. Codex recorded the third tool result as `isError=true` with `OpenClaw dynamic tool call aborted.`

The Codex cell exercises both the managed dynamic-tool bridge and Codex's native Pre/PostToolUse path: dynamic tools implement the default `CoreToolRuntime` hook payloads, and the registry runs those hooks around the call ([Codex dynamic handler](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs), [Codex registry](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/registry.rs#L490-L603)). Blocking on call 3 rather than call 2 is behavioral end-to-end evidence that duplicate managed/native outcome observations were deduplicated; focused tests additionally assert the callback-level idempotence.

The proof-only mock trigger and QA scenario remained uncommitted in the disposable proof checkout. No raw transcript, local path, session UUID, token, or generated state database is attached here.

### Deterministic and review proof

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.critical-tool-loop.test.ts`: 7/7 passed. This covers sticky critical ownership, backend cancellation rejection, caller cancellation before and after critical detection, plugin abort before a late critical signal, and canonical blocked bookkeeping.
- Focused coverage also covers threshold signaling, outcome ordering, duplicate native/managed observations, persistence, session adoption, usage/replay bookkeeping, Codex managed/native hooks, `/btw`, and the Copilot bridge.
- Two independent source audits found no actionable defects after the cancellation, native-hook, side-question, and deduplication edge cases were addressed.
- Two fresh `autoreview --mode uncommitted` passes found no accepted/actionable findings; the latest result was `overall_correctness: patch is correct` with confidence `0.97`.
- Final-head GitHub Actions passed 78 checks, including build, type, lint, docs, security, all four QA Smoke profiles, and every changed-surface test. The only primary failure is an unchanged process-timing test: `src/process/child-process.test.ts` expected descendant output `TICK6` but observed only `HEAD`; `openclaw/ci-gate` is its derivative failure. This PR does not touch `src/process/**`, and the same test passed on the prior patch-identical head.

### Dependency contract

Checked directly against `openai/codex@2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3`: [`success: false` dynamic-tool responses remain normal tool outputs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs), and native pre/post hooks share the tool call identity and response lifecycle ([registry dispatch](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/registry.rs#L490-L603)).

target.title: fix(infra): bound warning dedup caches with createDedupeCache
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Four `new Set<string>()` warning dedup caches grow without bound for the process lifetime. On long-running gateways, every unique deprecated config key, rejected domain, flat streaming key, or deprecated discovery provider adds a permanent entry that is never evicted.

## Fix

Replace each unbounded `Set<string>` with `createDedupeCache({ maxSize: 4096, ttlMs: 0 })`. The `check()` method combines `has()`+`add()` into one size-bounded operation. When the cache exceeds 4096 entries, the oldest half is evicted.

Existing behavior unchanged: each warning fires once per cache window. Test-only `clear()` helpers continue to work. Follows #101746 and #109000.

## Evidence

### Caller-level function probe (real production warning path)

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import { warnFlatStreamingKeyFallback } from ./src/channels/streaming-flat-key-deprecation.js"

1. First call with "chunkMode":
   [streaming] Flat channel streaming key "chunkMode" is deprecated;
   move it to streaming.chunkMode. The flat fallback is removed after the next release train.
   → warning fired (check() returned false)

2. Second call with "chunkMode":
   → warning suppressed (check() returned true)
```

### Overflow + re-warning proof (maxSize=3 for demonstration)

```
check("a"): NEW — warning fires
check("b"): NEW — warning fires
check("c"): NEW — warning fires
check("d"): NEW — warning fires  (a evicted)
check("e"): NEW — warning fires  (b evicted)

After overflow:
peek("a"): evicted — can warn again
peek("b"): evicted — can warn again
peek("c"): cached
peek("d"): cached
peek("e"): cached
```

### Vitest output (48/48 tests pass, 5 files)

```
$ npx vitest run src/plugins/provider-validation.test.ts \
  src/channels/streaming-flat-key-deprecation.test.ts \
  src/plugins/runtime/runtime-config.test.ts \
  src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.test.ts \
  src/infra/dedupe.test.ts

```

## Test plan

- [x] First call fires warning, second call with same key suppressed (caller-level)
- [x] Cache evicts oldest half when exceeding maxSize
- [x] Evicted keys can be warned again (bounded window, not permanent silence)

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `tool_choice` constraint is set (e.g. `tool_choice: { type: "function", name: "search" }`), a `replace: true, text: "..."` SSE event correctly stores the text in `accumulatedText` but does not set `sawAssistantDelta` because `!toolChoiceConstraint` blocks the guard at line 1059. If the stream ends without `tool_calls` (error/interruption), the non-streaming fallback at line 1277 selects content from `resultPayloadText || bufferedReplaceableAssistantContent` — neither includes the buffered text, so it is silently lost.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.body:
## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`
